metadata.title: Ways To Check How Good Your Memory Is
metadata.description: Try simple word, story, number and everyday-detail challenges to explore how you remember information, with practical tips and an answer guide.

landing.popupTitle: Most Adults Cannot Pass This Test
landing.title: Ways To Check How Good Your Memory Is
landing.adNote: One short ad, then read the article.

introduction: A familiar name slips away. You walk into a room and forget why. But how well can you remember something when you deliberately put your mind to it? Try these word, number and story challenges, then see which details stayed with you.
You will need a little paper and somewhere quiet. Take your time: these are informal activities for curiosity and general learning, not a medical assessment or a way to diagnose a memory condition.
gallery.completeCopy: Look at the kinds of details you remembered rather than treating one activity as a verdict. Try a fresh set another day if you enjoyed the challenge.

items.title: Start With Five Ordinary Words
paragraphs: Read this list: ANCHOR — CANDLE — LEMON — MIRROR — RABBIT. Give yourself enough time to notice each word, then move on without writing the list down. There is no countdown.
We will come back to these words later. For now, the challenge is simply to carry them with you while your attention moves to something else. Avoid scrolling back once you begin the other activities.

items.title: Try the Tabletop Snapshot
paragraphs: Place five safe everyday objects on a table. Study the arrangement, then cover the objects with a cloth. Write down what was there without lifting the cloth.

Now add another layer: where was each object? You might remember a pen but not whether it sat beside the cup or near the edge. Record the object names and their positions separately, then uncover the table and check.

items.title: Read a Tiny Story Once
paragraphs: Here is the story: On Tuesday, Amira took a blue umbrella to the library and returned two books. Her friend Sam met her outside.
Read it carefully, then continue. Later, we will ask about the person, the day and a few other details. You do not need to rush, but try not to turn it into a written shopping list.

items.title: Turn a Short Number Sequence Around
paragraphs: Look at 3 — 8 — 1 — 6. Cover the sequence or move it off the screen, then write the numbers in reverse order.

This asks you to hold the sequence and rearrange it rather than simply copy it. Keep the task untimed. The answer guide near the end lets you check the exact order without a guess about whether you were close enough.

items.title: Attach Three Names to Three Objects
paragraphs: Remember these pairs: Ava has a compass. Ben has a pear. Leo has a hat. Picture each person holding their object, or quietly repeat the pairs if that feels easier.
Move on when you are ready. The later question will ask you to recover the links, not just remember that a compass, a pear and a hat appeared somewhere in the article.

items.title: Set Yourself a Small Future Task
paragraphs: When you reach the heading Final Recall, draw a star in the corner of your paper. Do not do it yet. The idea is to remember an intention when the right moment arrives.

For this first attempt, avoid adding a reminder. In everyday life, however, calendars, notes and alerts are useful tools, not something to feel guilty about using. This activity is only a small experiment.

items.title: Take a Familiar Route in Your Mind
paragraphs: Without looking at a map, describe a familiar walk from your front door to a nearby place. List a few landmarks in the order you would pass them. Stay where you are; there is no need to go out or drive anywhere.
Afterward, compare your description with a map or with someone who knows the route. Separate details you confidently recalled from details you filled in because they seemed plausible.

items.title: Make an Everyday List Less Random
paragraphs: Read these items: oats, grapes, pasta, soap, tea, rice, apples and shampoo. Cover the list and write down what you remember.

Next, look again and arrange the items into groups that make sense to you, such as food and bathroom supplies. Cover the list again and try recalling it by group. This is a way to explore a strategy, not a fair comparison of two separate scores: you have already seen the same items before.

items.title: Check a Detail You Usually Overlook
paragraphs: Choose a familiar room that you cannot currently see. Describe three details: perhaps the order of objects on a shelf, the position of a clock or the pattern on a cushion.

Then check the room. Notice whether an error came from forgetting something you had noticed or from never paying much attention to it in the first place. This exercise does not tell you why a mistake happened, but it gives you something concrete to compare.

items.title: Can You Bring Back the Five Words?
paragraphs: Without returning to the opening section, write down the five words from the first list. Any order is fine. Leave a space if a word will not come to you rather than filling it with a confident guess.

Keep this first attempt on your paper. If another word comes back to you later, note it separately so you can distinguish what you recalled now from what returned after more time. The answer guide appears further down.

items.title: Find Out Which Story Details Survived
paragraphs: Think back to the short story. Who went out? On which day? What colour was the umbrella? Where did the person go, how many books were returned and who met them outside?

Write your answers before checking. A story can leave a strong general impression even when individual details are harder to recover. Here, the point is to compare the details you actually remember with the ones you only assume.

items.title: Reconnect the Names and Objects
paragraphs: Who had the compass? Which object belonged to Ben? What was Leo holding? Try answering without returning to the pairs section.
If you remember all three objects but mix up their owners, record that distinction. It makes the exercise more interesting than treating every uncertain answer as the same kind of mistake.

items.title: Try a Two-Step Mental Shuffle
paragraphs: Study 4 — 7 — 2 — 9, then cover the sequence. Move the last number to the front. After that, swap the two middle numbers. Write the final sequence down.

Work slowly if you like. The challenge is keeping track of the changing order, not doing difficult arithmetic. If you lose your place, stop and record where the sequence became uncertain instead of turning the activity into a race.

items.title: Compare a Picture With a Description
paragraphs: Choose a simple, non-sensitive picture, such as a room or a landscape. Look at it, put it out of sight and describe several details in writing. If you prefer, ask someone to describe a different picture aloud and see what you can recall from their description.

Keep the two attempts separate. Different pictures, descriptions and amounts of study time make this an informal comparison, not evidence that one kind of memory is better than another. You are exploring what feels easier, not measuring a fixed ability.

items.title: Notice the Difference Between Recall and a Clue
paragraphs: Return to your written attempt at the five-word list, but do not change it. If an item was missing, try this clue: one word was a fruit. Does a particular answer return to you?

Mark any answer that needed the clue separately from your original attempt. Being prompted is a different experience from producing a word without help. Neither result, on its own, tells you whether you have a medical problem.

items.title: Final Recall
paragraphs: Before reading on, was there something you intended to do when this heading appeared? Give yourself a moment to think back to the earlier instruction.

The task was to draw a star in the corner of your paper. If you remembered without this reminder, note that. If you did not, treat it as one missed activity rather than a verdict on your everyday memory.

items.title: Look at Patterns, Not a Pass Mark
paragraphs: Compare the kinds of information you remembered: words, positions, names, story details or an instruction for later. You may find one activity comfortable and another unexpectedly awkward.

There is no validated pass mark, population ranking or diagnostic score for these homemade exercises. Difficulty, familiarity, distractions and how you approached each task all affect what the result means. Do not use this article to decide whether you have dementia or another condition.

items.title: Try a Fresh Version Another Day
paragraphs: If you enjoyed the activities, ask someone to make a different word list, short story and set of pairs for another occasion. Keep the instructions and study conditions similar if you want a more useful personal comparison.

Repeating the same material lets you learn the answers, so an improved attempt does not automatically show that your general memory has improved. Keep this as a curiosity exercise rather than a daily test you feel compelled to pass.

items.title: Check the Answers You Could Verify
paragraphs: The opening words were ANCHOR, CANDLE, LEMON, MIRROR and RABBIT. The reversed number sequence was 6 — 1 — 8 — 3. For the two-step shuffle, moving 9 to the front gives 9 — 4 — 7 — 2; swapping the middle pair then gives 9 — 7 — 4 — 2.

In the story, Amira went to the library on Tuesday with a blue umbrella, returned two books and met Sam outside. The pairs were Ava with a compass, Ben with a pear and Leo with a hat. The later instruction was to draw a star when you reached Final Recall.
For the table, room, route and picture activities, compare your notes with the actual objects or a reliable reference. Do not invent a single overall score by combining very different tasks.

items.title: When a Game Is Not Enough
paragraphs: Occasional forgetfulness does not by itself establish a diagnosis. Stress, anxiety, depression and sleeping problems can be associated with memory difficulties. If memory problems are recurring or affecting your day-to-day life, arrange an appointment with a healthcare professional rather than relying on an online challenge.

Bring specific examples of what has changed and, if helpful, someone who can describe what they have noticed. The NHS advises against trying to diagnose the cause of memory loss yourself. The resources below explain when to seek advice and what an assessment may involve.
